turn_text: There is never, never a shortage of issues to talk about in Washington D.C. United States Representative Sharice David, the Democrat from Kansas City, Kansas knows that well. Welcome to the Kansas Reflector Podcast.

Well, I mean, it's obviously. I would say egregious. And it's also heartbreaking to see the suffering that's going on. And when President Zelensky addressed the Congress last week, he shared some video images of some of the damage that is happening in Ukraine. I think, first of all, I am really, really glad to see that the US and our allies are coming together and imposing sanctions and increasing the cost and the pressure on Russia for what is a completely unjustified aggression. And I think that, you know, The desire is there and it this is one of those areas where we're seeing bipartisan support to keep up the sanctions and to make sure that we're doing what we can to put economic pressure on them, while at the same time, where, you know, doing what we can in terms of support through efforts to help them keep themselves safe, whether it's some of the aid and assistance that we're going to be sending over to humanitarian aid and also military aid.

turn_text: So I think, speaking of restraint and limitations, I think there's a movement in Congress to try to make it so that members can't do a lot of stock trading. Trust in Congress Act, perhaps it's called.
What's your
view on that?

Well, a couple of things. One is just for folks who might not have heard about it, that specific bill, because there's a number of bills out there. This one is the Trust in Congress Act. It's a bipartisan bill that would require members of Congress, senators included, to put certain investment stocks and that sort of thing into a qualified blind trust during the entire time that a person would serve in Congress. And it basically would create a firewall that I hope will help people have more trust in our institutions of government. I think we've seen that that's at an all time low. And then this bill also would require the rules would apply to spouses and independent children of electeds.
So you think it's a necessary step at this juncture?

Well, I think, I mean, I definitely think it's a good idea. And I guess, you know, if you look at the last few years, we saw just, I mean, just the last few years, we saw too many instances where we saw questionable kind of financial conduct by elected officials, members, and senators. If you think back to when COVID was first emerging, we saw some trades by electeds or their spouses that bind things like pharmaceutical stocks and other tech-related stocks before the public really had an understanding of what was going on with COVID. I think regardless of whether or not any laws at that time were broken, it was clearly uh, inappropriate at, at a minimum. And, um, and I think that, you know, people need to be able to trust that, that we're here to serve in the public interest. And, you know, we have a, we have a big responsibility and people need to be able to trust that we're making our decisions and doing things in a way that's good for our constituents.
